cues: Welcome to Claude Agents — the complete visual guide.
Prepared by Sara Salem.
In this video, you'll learn what an AI agent really is, how Claude works as an agent, and how to build your own agent — step by step, from the first idea to production.
Let's start with the difference between a chatbot and an agent.
A chatbot answers one message at a time. You ask, it replies, and then it waits for you. It can't take action in the world on its own.
An agent is different. You give it a goal, and it plans the work, uses tools, takes actions, checks the results, and keeps going until the job is done.
In short: a chatbot talks. An agent gets things done.
So, what exactly is an agent?
A simple definition: an agent is a language model, like Claude, using tools in a loop, to work toward a goal with a high degree of independence.
Claude is the brain. It reasons, plans, and decides what to do next.
Tools are its hands — searching the web, reading files, running code, or calling your company's systems.
And context, memory, and guardrails keep it informed, focused, and safe.
At the heart of every agent is a loop. Anthropic describes it in a few simple stages.
First, gather context. The agent searches, reads files, and collects the information it needs.
Second, take action. It uses tools — writing code, editing a document, or calling an API.
Third, verify the work. It checks the result — running tests, comparing against rules, or reviewing its own output.
And then, repeat. The loop continues until the goal is reached, or until a human needs to step in.
Every agent is built from four core building blocks.
The model: Claude, providing reasoning and planning.
Tools: the actions the agent can take, from built-in tools to your own custom functions and MCP connections.
Context and memory: instructions, files, and knowledge the agent can draw on during its work.
And guardrails: permissions, limits, and human approvals that keep the agent safe and under control.
Not every problem needs a fully autonomous agent. Anthropic's guide to building effective agents describes several proven patterns, from simple workflows to full agents.
Prompt chaining splits a task into fixed steps, where each step's output feeds the next.
Routing classifies the input first, then sends it to the best specialized path.
Parallelization runs several sub-tasks at the same time, then combines the results.
Orchestrator and workers: a lead model breaks down the task, and delegates pieces to worker models — like subagents.
Evaluator and optimizer: one model creates, another reviews and gives feedback, in a loop.
And finally, the autonomous agent: Claude decides its own steps, using tools in a loop. Start with the simplest pattern that works, and add complexity only when it helps.
Where can you use Claude as an agent today?
Claude Code is an agent for software work. It reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and verifies its changes.
In the Claude apps, features like Research and Cowork let Claude work through multi-step tasks for you.
The Claude Agent SDK gives developers the same agent foundation that powers Claude Code, to build their own agents.
And the Claude API lets you design a custom agent loop from scratch, using tool use.
Now, let's build an agent, step by step. Step one: define the job.
A good agent task has several steps, needs tools or data, and has a clear definition of done — so the agent knows when it has succeeded.
Some tasks are not a good fit yet: simple one-shot questions, goals with no clear finish line, or risky actions that can't be undone without human review.
Write down the goal, the inputs, the expected output, and how you'll measure success. This becomes your agent's mission.
Step two: set up your environment with the Claude Agent SDK.
First, install the SDK. It's available for Python and for TypeScript.
Second, add your API key from the Claude Console, as an environment variable.
Third, choose where your agent will run — on your laptop while you build, and later on a server or in a container.
And fourth, run a quick test to make sure everything is connected.
Step three: write your first agent.
Start with the instructions, in a system prompt. Tell the agent who it is, what its goal is, and how it should work.
Next, decide which tools it's allowed to use. Begin with a small, safe set — for example, reading and searching files.
Set limits, like the maximum number of turns, so the agent can't run forever.
Then send it a task, and stream back its messages as it works. You can watch every step it takes.
Step four: give your agent custom tools, so it can work with your own systems.
Define a tool with a clear name and a description. The description tells Claude when the tool is useful.
Describe the input the tool expects — here, a customer ID.
Inside the function, connect to your real system, such as your CRM or database, and return the result.
Finally, register the tool with your agent and allow it. Now Claude can call it whenever it needs that information.
Step five: give your agent the right context and memory.
Level one is instructions. A project file, like CLAUDE dot M D, can hold your rules, style, and background knowledge.
Level two is knowledge on demand: files, documents, and search tools the agent can use to find information when it needs it.
Level three is memory over time. For long tasks, the agent can keep notes and summaries, and older context can be compacted, so it stays focused.
The goal is simple: give the agent exactly what it needs — no more, no less.
Step six: add guardrails and permissions. Let's follow what happens when the agent wants to take an action.
First, the agent decides it wants to use a tool.
Then a permission check confirms whether that tool is allowed at all.
Next, hooks can run your own rules automatically — for example, blocking changes to sensitive files.
For high-impact actions, a human can review and approve before anything happens.
Only then is the action executed, and every step can be logged for review.
Step seven: test and evaluate your agent. This is what turns a demo into a reliable product.
Build a set of realistic test tasks, with clear pass and fail criteria.
Run the agent on every version, and track the results — like the pass rate, the cost per task, and the number of turns it takes.
In this illustrative example, each improvement to the instructions and tools raises the pass rate, version after version.
Look closely at the failures. They show you exactly what to improve next.
Step eight: deploy and monitor your agent.
Run it where it belongs — on a server, in a container, or inside your app — with secure access to its tools.
Observe everything it does, with logs and traces of each step and tool call.
Control costs and risks, with usage limits, timeouts, and alerts.
And keep improving. Real-world feedback becomes new test cases, and the cycle continues.
So, what kinds of agents can you build? Here are some ideas.
A coding agent that fixes bugs and writes tests. A research agent that gathers and summarizes sources. And a customer support agent that resolves tickets.
A finance agent that reconciles accounts. A data analyst agent that answers questions with real numbers. And an operations agent that automates routine work.
Plus a sales assistant that prepares account briefs, and a personal productivity agent that manages your inbox and calendar.
Before we finish, here are six best practices for building great agents.
One: start simple. Use the simplest pattern that solves the problem.
Two: write clear instructions, and clear tool descriptions.
Three: give the minimum permissions needed, and expand carefully.
Four: keep a human in the loop for important or irreversible actions.
Five: measure everything, with evaluations, logs, and costs.
And six: iterate. Every failure is a lesson for the next version.
Let's recap in one line: plan, act, verify.
Claude agents use tools in a loop to reach real goals — and with the right steps, instructions, and guardrails, you can build one for your own work.
